title: SLA & fallback cost playbook (seller quick reference)
content:
Purpose:
Quick reference for sellers and SEs to 1) position Redwood SLAs and fallback strategies to reduce deal risk 2) frame cost tradeoffs for reserved capacity vs. fallback routing and 3) run a fast technical check during pilot conversations. Draft / working — many TODOs below.

High-level pitch (30s):
- Redwood gives product teams predictable inference with clear latency SLOs + built-in graceful degradation.
- If primary model or zone is constrained, automated routing + cheaper quantized variants keep calls running (controlled quality tradeoff) — we treat that as a feature, not a failure.

Key buyer personas / talking points:
- Platform/Infra Architect: talk throughput guarantees, isolation (Dedicated pools) and routing controls. Show burst policies and autoscale windows.
- Product/ML Engineer: emphasize canary routing, model variant grading, and eval hooks to detect quality regressions.
- Procurement / Finance: frame unit economics (per-token vs reserved capacity) and show break-even scenarios.

Common objections + short rebuttals (scripts):
1) "We can't risk degraded outputs during peak times."
  - Script: "Understandable — we set deterministic fallback rules (model variant + region) and expose a simulated SLO breach log so you can see exactly when fallbacks would have applied in your traffic patterns. We can also pin critical routes to a non-fallback dedicated pool for X% of traffic (customers do this for payment flows)."
2) "Reserved capacity is expensive compared to on-demand."
  - Script: "For sustained throughput, reserved yields predictable cost and lower p50/p90 latency. We provide a 90‑day usage simulation from your sample traces to show exact $/1000 token delta. Short answer: pilots often start on hosted; when sustained, reserved usually saves 30–60% depending on burstiness."
3) "How do we verify quality when fallback occurs?"
  - Script: "We run prompt regression evals and send alerts tied to prompt sets. You get diffs and sample outputs; plus, fallbacks can be routed to a staging variant first for canarying."

SLA & fallback design patterns (starter reference):
- Primary route: latest recommended model (e.g., redwood-14b-ops). Latency SLO 150ms p95 for short prompts.
- Fallback 1: quantized 14b variant (same arch, ~3–7% quality delta, 30–40% cost reduction).
- Fallback 2: small-ensemble fast model (higher hallucination risk, 60% cheaper).
- Region failover: route to secondary region if latency/availability drops below threshold.
- Policy order: Primary -> Quant variant -> Region fallback -> Cheap fast model -> 503/queue (if configured to preserve correctness).

Seller cheat-sheet: when to recommend which configuration
- Pilot / proof-of-value: hosted API default; enable light KV caching, set soft p95 SLOs, no reserved commit. Add cost cap alert.
- Production-critical flows (payments, auth): recommend Dedicated + pinned routes + synchronous alerting + stronger SLAs.
- Burst-tolerant UIs: enable autoscale with burst credits; configure graceful degrade to lighter model when queue grows > X.

Quick math example (for calls-level economics)
- Customer sample: 10M tokens / month, avg prompt length 50 tokens.
- Hosted per-token baseline: $0.0005 / token -> $5,000/mo.
- Reserved (committed) expected unit $0.00032 -> $3,200/mo.
- If we enable quantized fallback for 25% of tokens: effective spend = 0.75*0.00032 + 0.25*0.0002 = $0.000284 -> savings vs hosted = ~43%.
- Note: swap numbers with real price list and include frictional commitments.

Technical pre-sale checklist (run live or ask customer to share traces):
- Obtain invocation trace (sample of 1k requests): check seq len distribution, token split prompt/response, p95 latency targets.
- Identify hot routes (top 10 endpoints) -> suggest per-route SLOs and cache keys.
- Suggest quantization profile candidate: which models tolerate 4-bit or int8 for workload?
- Draft rollback policy: how to quickly unpin fallback routing if quality alerts show regressions.

Canary / rollout plan (seller + SE talking points):
1) Stage canary: 5% traffic -> 24h metrics + prompt-diff alerts -> manual approval.
2) Ramp: 25% -> compare embedding similarity / quality metrics -> metrics hold if regression > threshold.
3) Go-wide: move to desired split or reserved pin.

Deck outline (for a compact 6-slide pitch)
- Slide 1: One-liner + customer logo placeholders + problem statement (inference unpredictability)
- Slide 2: How Redwood serves: runtime + smart routing + fallback overview (diagram placeholder)
- Slide 3: SLA/fallback policy examples + cost impact mini-table
- Slide 4: Pilot plan + technical checklist (ask for traces)
- Slide 5: Objection Q&A (short scripts)
- Slide 6: Next steps + call to action (pilot request link / dedicated trial form)

Unresolved / TODOs for SEs & GTM:
- Add real price tiers and a small table for quick onsite calculation (Rachel to provide price matrix).
- Validate quantization delta numbers with Applied ML (Mina).
- Build a one-click simulation tool for seller UI (connected to usage simulator) — spike JIRA: JIRA-GTM-6789.
- Create a short recording (3–4m) for new sellers walking through the 6-slide deck.

Notes to self (Aisha):
- Keep language concrete, avoid generic "fail-safe" wording. Customers care about exact behaviors.
- Follow up with Solutions Eng for 2 customer example case studies (one high-compliance, one consumer app).

Appendix snippets (copyable)
- Email to SE: "Can you run a 1k-sample trace and return p50/p95 and seq length histogram? We'll model reserved savings and propose an SLO split for 30/60/90 day rollout."
- Quick value sentence for finance: "Switching to reserved when steady throughput exists typically reduces per-token cost by ~30–50% while giving predictable latency and capacity guarantees."

End.
